Higher Efficiency thin film solar cells
Supervisors
Professor Stephen Sweeney
Application deadline: 31/1/24 for a School/EPSRC Scholarship
Description
Solar panels based on photovoltaics are becoming a common sight and are an important route to delivering renewable energy and minimising carbon emissions. Solar panels found their first major use in space, where they continue to be the main source of power generation onboard satellites. However, terrestrial and space applications place very different demands on the solar panels; for space applications, high efficiency, low mass and reliability are key, whereas roof-top solar panels are much more sensitive to cost and typically use materials that are intrinsically less efficient and simpler to produce. This project aims to develop photovoltaic solar cell approaches that can provide advantages in both efficiency, mass and cost by focusing on the development of new semiconductor materials and heterostructures, based on the bismide-nitride family of III-V semiconductors.
Two PhD projects are available in this topic. The first project will undertake a theoretical exploration of the properties of the semiconductors and how manipulation of the electronic band structure can lead to high absorption within very thin layers. The project will work from electronic band structure calculations, through to modelling of photovoltaic device performance. The second project will aim to experimentally demonstrate the influence of band structure on photovoltaic efficiency and will work with collaborative partners to demonstrate prototype semiconductor alloys and devices.

Description
Wireless communications are mainstream and we are constantly surrounded by electromagnetic waves wirelessly transmitting large volumes of data. However, almost all the technologies that we use at some point require plugging-in to charge. Wireless inductive charging for mobile phones is now becoming standard. However, it requires very close proximity to a charging point, limiting range. If energy could be delivered as seamlessly as data it would open-up many applications ranging from powering small sensors over a few metres, through to mobile phones, laptops etc. anywhere within a room, electric vehicles on the roads and ultimately delivering energy within space over 1000s km. Optical-based approaches offer a potential solution owing to the relative ease of beaming a focused beam of energy using lasers.

Supervisors

Description
Temperature is one of the most familiar measurable quantities that influences our lives. It is also a key quantity controlling chemical processes, for example in the body, or in the manufacture of chemicals and pharmaceuticals. It also impacts the functionality and efficiency of many technologies and controlling heat generation and flow, for example in processor chips is key to optimising their performance and energy use.
Current ways of measuring temperature suffer from two main issues: (i) the need for periodic calibration to a “known” traceable standard to avoid drift, and (ii) the challenge of measuring temperature on a sub-micron scale, e.g. inside electronic chips. Terahertz Sources and Detectors with On-chip Metamaterial-enabled Antennas
Supervisors: Professor Edward Wasige, Professor David Cumming and Dr Vincenzo Pusino
The terahertz (THz) frequency band, especially beyond 0.3 THz where 100 GHz wide transmission windows are available, provide large bandwidths which can support extremely high data rate wireless communication, while the short wavelengths provide sensitivity to texture for high fidelity contrasted imagery. THz waves also possess the unique property of penetrating opaque materials such as composites, ceramics, textiles, and polymers as well as volumetric obscurants, and so provide the capability to characterise in a reliable and contactless manner the internal structure of such materials and media. This is of great value to the aerospace sector for composite material inspections and to civil engineering for monitoring defects, deterioration processes in construction materials and probe the propagation channels on the presence of obscurants. Current THz technologies are, however, too bulky, energy-demanding, delicate and expensive with some requiring cryogenic cooling, which prevents their wide adoption and applications other than for scientific instruments.
This PhD project aims to research and develop compact, energy-efficient (battery-operated), low-cost (hundreds of pounds), and high performance (e.g. ³ 10 mW at 0.425 THz) sources and highly sensitive (e.g. noise equivalent power (NEP) £ 0.1 pW/√Hz) detectors operating at room temperature. It will build on the extensive research in THz resonant tunnelling diode (RTD) technology and in THz metamaterial-based detectors at the University of Glasgow by coalescing and harmonising the technical approaches into a unified THz integrated circuit technology platform. The project provides an excellent opportunity to pioneer the development of a high-performance technology for emerging applications with huge societal relevance.

Mergemon-Based Superconducting Circuits: A Joint JWNC–SQMS Coherence Engineering Project
Description
This PhD project will advance next-generation superconducting qubits based on trilayer niobium Josephson junction technology (“mergemons”), building on recent breakthroughs at the James Watt Nanofabrication Centre (JWNC) and in collaboration with the SQMS Center at Fermilab. The trilayer Nb process developed at Glasgow provides exceptionally clean interfaces, enhanced coherence, and robust frequency designability. Mergemons, or merged-element transmons, are a type of superconducting qubit used in quantum computing that features a significantly reduced physical size compared to conventional transmons. The student will exploit this platform to realise and characterise novel mergemon-type qubits and coupled-mode quantum circuits optimised for long lifetimes in packaging environments.
Fabrication will be performed at the JWNC using the established niobium trilayer process, enabling reproducible, scalable junctions and complex multi-qubit layouts. Device packaging and advanced integration will leverage the existing infrastructure and the university’s emerging capabilities in 2.5D/3D superconducting interconnects. Measurements will be undertaken in the Quantum Circuit Group using FPGA-based, cryogenic-compatible control systems and high-efficiency readout chains, with extended measurement campaigns at SQMS to probe coherence limits, materials loss mechanisms, and noise spectroscopy under cryogenic and circuit-QED conditions.
The student will join a joint Glasgow–SQMS team, contributing to collaborative studies on materials-processing correlations, energy-participation modelling, and the scalability of multilayer superconducting circuits. The outcome will be a validated mergemon architecture demonstrating improved coherence and manufacturability, strengthening UK–US collaboration and providing a fabrication-ready qubit technology for future quantum processors.
